Hermes Agent can now review your codebase for security bugs with the new official Security plugin by @mark_s.

Hermes first maps what an attacker could reach and which inputs it trusts. It splits the code across parallel subagents, checks every candidate finding against the code, and traces whether an attacker can actually exploit it.

Turn on test confirmation and Hermes writes a small reproduction for each finding and runs it in a temporary copy of the repo. Each report records the evidence and the findings Hermes ruled out, and exports to SARIF for your existing tools.

Run it from chat, the CLI, or the Security page in Hermes Desktop.

"Hinted Scaling Laws"

Scaling laws can predict how LLMs improve with scale, how do you predict a larger model's performance on difficult benchmarks when all the smaller models score nearly zero?

This paper introduces Hinted Scaling Laws, which gives smaller models varying amounts of help, such as partial solutions, to reveal how their accuracy improves. Researchers then use these patterns to predict larger models' performance without hints.

Across GSM8K, AIME, and HLE, this reduces median forecasting error from 21 to 4.3%, making predictions of future model capabilities much more accurate.

https://t.co/xVCvMka7Kd

"VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding"

Generating visual plans for robotics and autonomous driving models is done one coordinate at a time, making detailed trajectories slow to produce.

NVIDIA's new paper VFlash proposes a lightweight diffusion model to predict entire trajectories, bounding boxes, and 3D motion in parallel, rather than generating each coordinate sequentially.

This reduces robot planning latency by around 80% while improving spatial accuracy. 

On MolmoSpaces, robot task success improves from 62.6% to 70.2% when an action model uses VFlash's plans.

https://t.co/vv9cpGlo9k

Built a physical simulation of a record player with WebGL2 and Web Audio. It's *shockingly* accurate: https://t.co/MBNaTfKoai.

Instead of playing a song, it works by converting it into the physical shape of a groove. Then a simulated stylus rides those walls 384,000 times a second, and you hear the voltage that motion would induce in a cartridge.

So the crackle, the pops, the wow/flutter, the dull inner grooves are natural byproducts of the simulation. You can also "DJ" the record.

(The converted songs are in the public domain or CC-licensed. Code is linked for you to remix and re-deploy.)

tweets.text:
We’re moving from an era of AI where the output comes roughly at the rate that you can chat back and forth with the AI to work with you, to a period where you can set a problem for a set of agents to go off and do an arbitrarily large amount of work for you. This means productivity gains that are maybe 20-50% to gains that don’t really have an upper limit.

Agent swarms and the ability to fan out complex work across many agents doing tasks in parallel provide a massive unlock in a lot of spaces. This will lead to qualitatively different outcomes in my fields. 

This has already been seen across the coding domain. Next, cyber is almost entirely a problem space where more agents reviewing more things will lead to far better outcomes. We’re seeing the same now in many scientific fields, and this almost certainly will change life sciences. 

But this will increasingly be true in any field where you can parallelize computer-based work to complete something faster or do something at a totally different quality level. Which is actually are some of the most valuable domains of knowledge work today. 

Our brains aren’t really wired for the new scenario we’re heading into where compute becomes the variable that we can flex to solve any problem that we want. We’re used to thinking that the amount of time that goes into a task is correlated to the output that we get from it. And most domains of knowledge work or science have generally always been correlated with this. That’s changing forever.

A good lesson in AI is that you need to check back in on the latest with every 3 to 6 months to try something that wasn’t possible before and see if it works again.

At no point in AI’s history is that more true than today. Just the past six months of model progress around computer and tool use, less context rot, better reasoning, multimodality, and deeper domain expertise in a number of key fields, these models are vastly more capable on what they can execute.

This is opening up a new vector of what AI systems will be able to autonomously work on. Essentially, anything with an API (and even many things without), we can anticipate that an agent will be able to control and utilize as an underlying capability to complete a process.

This means that we are no longer dependent on *just* the models generating everything from whole cloth, but instead they can fully utilize existing systems (or new ones purpose built for them) very effectively. This creates immense leverage for agents.

Security agents can leverage existing data feeds and cyber tooling, IT agents that can execute workflows reliably across software stacks, data agents that can migrate data or processes between systems, architect and design agents can leverage CAD and design tools, and on and on. And any of today’s tools that don’t work will likely be replaced by agent-friendly or OSS tooling that does the same. 

When you combine this with the domain understanding being trained into agents, you started to get autonomous collaborators for every job function and industry. This will open up a ton of new opportunities in AI if you build with this understanding in mind.

If you are visiting SF, and trying to meet more people, here are a random list of things you should remove from your vocabulary..

> swap notes
> "synergies"
> pick your brain
> networking
> "san fran" (tourist tell)
> grab coffee if you're free

If you want to meet interesting people here, show your work. The most interesting people I know in the city are not attending that fancy large conference - they are probably at their office. 

So what's the work? It can be as simple as a thoughtful cold email, a five line pointed DM, or complex as some side projects that you have shipped, or a meetup that you are organizing.

If you put in the effort, it shows, yes, even in this AI era. I still get so much slop across the board, that if I see anyone put in the effort, I try to go out of my way to meet them. 

Even the busiest people have 15 mins to give you, if you give them a reason to!

A company you’ve never heard of was started 10yrs ago is the 32nd largest in the world.

They are the #4 largest maker of DRAM, behind Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron with ~10% of the global market. They’re worth $430B and were briefly the biggest company in China.

It’s ChanXin Memory Technologies (CXMT).

They’re growing >6x YoY, and made $40B in the first 9mos of this year at 50% gross margin. Surprisingly, 2/3rd of its business is phone memory, and AI compute is a small part of their business.

The founder, Yiming Zhu did his PhD at Stony Brook after Tsinghua and worked in semis in the valley before going back to China in 2005. He started CXMT in 2016 in the lesser known city of Hefei.

The funding story of the company is unusually fascinating too. The city government of Hefei owns ~37% of the business after providing physical city resides and eating losses on it for 10yrs! We think about VCs backing companies in the US, but in China, governments can too.
